full_text_en:
People's Insurance Company of China, Zhejiang Branch v. Guangzhou Ocean Shipping Company and China National Foreign Trade Transportation Corporation, Shanghai Branch — dispute over maritime cargo transport contract and agency

Plaintiff: People's Insurance Company of China, Zhejiang Branch.

Legal Representative: Dai Fengju, General Manager.

Agent ad litem: Jin Zuguang, Attorney at Shanghai Maritime Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Zhao Xuefang, Staff Member of the Second Export Section, People's Insurance Company of China, Zhejiang Branch.

Defendant: Guangzhou Ocean Shipping Company.

Legal Representative: Ye Guangwei, Manager.

Agent ad litem: Huang Zhengquan, Head of Protection and Indemnity Section, Attorney at Guangzhou Ocean Shipping Company.

Agent ad litem: Fang Jiadong, Staff Member of Protection and Indemnity Section, Guangzhou Ocean Shipping Company.

Defendant: China National Foreign Trade Transportation Corporation, Shanghai Branch.

Legal Representative: Huang Xinsheng, General Manager.

Agent ad litem: Wu Shulin, Hu Qinfu, Attorneys at Shanghai Baiyulan Law Firm.

The Plaintiff, People's Insurance Company of China, Zhejiang Branch (hereinafter referred to as Zhejiang Branch), instituted an action before the Shanghai Maritime Court against the Defendants, Guangzhou Ocean Shipping Company (hereinafter referred to as Ocean Shipping Company) and China National Foreign Trade Transportation Corporation, Shanghai Branch (hereinafter referred to as Shanghai Branch), concerning a dispute over a maritime cargo transport contract and agency.

Plaintiff's Allegations

The Plaintiff Zhejiang Branch alleged: When the Defendant Ocean Shipping Company carried the 750 cases of Chinese black tea insured by the Plaintiff, it provided unclean containers, and the Defendant Shanghai Branch, as the loading party, failed to perform a proper inspection, resulting in the tainting and contamination of the tea by odors. The Plaintiff compensated the consignee for the losses. The Plaintiff requested the two Defendants to compensate the Plaintiff for all economic losses of £7,476.63 and 1,881 German marks, together with interest from the date of the Plaintiff's compensation to the consignee until the date of judgment, and to bear all litigation costs.

Defendant's Defense

The Defendant Ocean Shipping Company argued: The container transport terms under this bill of lading were FCL (Full Container Load), i.e., the shipper loaded, counted, and sealed the full container. The container provided by the Defendant should be regarded as the packaging of the goods, and inspection of the container body should be the responsibility of the shipper. Moreover, the cause of the contamination was unclear, and the Plaintiff's compensation to the consignee was too hasty; its fairness remained to be determined. The Defendant would not bear liability for losses not caused by its own fault, and requested the Plaintiff to compensate it for the economic losses incurred from responding to the lawsuit.

The Defendant Shanghai Branch argued: The Defendant was entrusted by the shipper to perform container loading operations and was only responsible for the loading process, not for losses occurring thereafter. According to practice, the carrier should provide clean, dry, and odor-free containers, and the law does not require the container to be inspected. It should not bear liability for unforeseeable losses.

Facts Found by the Court

The Shanghai Maritime Court found: In 1987, the shipper, China National Native Produce and Animal By-Products Import and Export Corporation, Zhejiang Tea Branch, entrusted Zhejiang Qiantang Foreign Trade Transportation Corporation to export 750 cases of black tea from Shanghai to the port of Hamburg, West Germany. Qiantang Foreign Trade Transportation Corporation further sub-entrusted the Defendant Shanghai Branch to handle the export. After accepting the entrustment, Shanghai Branch applied for shipping space through Shanghai Ocean Shipping Agency. Shanghai Ocean Shipping Agency, acting as agent for the Defendant Ocean Shipping Company, assigned three 20-foot containers, including container number HTMU-5005420. Since the transport conditions were FCL, Shanghai Branch, as the shipper's agent, was fully responsible for counting, stowing, inspecting the containers, and affixing seals. On October 15 of that year, Shanghai Ocean Shipping Agency, after receiving the three fully loaded containers, issued a clean bill of lading on behalf of the vessel. Meanwhile, the shipper insured with the Plaintiff Zhejiang Branch for war risks and all risks under a marine cargo insurance policy.

Upon arrival of the goods in Hamburg, the consignee, upon opening the containers, discovered that some of the tea had been tainted and had deteriorated. The consignee immediately applied to BURMESTER·DUNCKER&JOLY, the Plaintiff's agent in Hamburg, for inspection. BURMESTER·DUNCKER&JOLY, acting as the survey and claims settling agent for the overseas marine insurance company, appointed Mr. Uwe Berner of HBGH Company to inspect the goods, and KRSP Chemical Laboratory conducted specialized testing. The inspection revealed that 250 cases of black tea had been contaminated by refined naphthalene. Consequently, the Plaintiff's agent in Hamburg compensated the consignee for losses of £7,476.63 and 1,881 German marks. A representative of the vessel was also present during the inspection of the goods. Additionally, it was further ascertained that one of the containers used for shipping the tea on this voyage, container number HTMU-5005420, had carried refined naphthalene on a previous voyage from Dunkirk, France to Shanghai. The above facts are confirmed by evidence including the export tea invoice of China National Native Produce and Animal By-Products Import and Export Corporation, Zhejiang Tea Branch, the bill of lading issued by Shanghai Ocean Shipping Agency, the transport insurance certificate of People's Insurance Company of China, the letter of subrogation signed by the consignee, and the survey reports from BURMESTER·DUNCKER&JOLY in Hamburg, West Germany, and other specialized inspection agencies.

Opinion of the Court

The Shanghai Maritime Court held: The identities of the parties were clear: the Defendant Ocean Shipping Company as the carrier providing the containers, the Defendant Shanghai Branch as the shipper's loading agent, and the Plaintiff as the insurer that obtained the right to claim under the letter of subrogation. The identity of BURMESTER·DUNCKER&JOLY as the survey and claims settling agent of the overseas marine insurance company, registered with the Hamburg Chamber of Commerce and in the Commercial Register of the Hamburg District Court, was clear. The transport insurance certificate issued by the Plaintiff expressly stated: "In the event of loss or damage to the insured goods, immediately notify our agent BURMESTER·DUNCKER&JOLY for survey." Therefore, it was beyond reproach for the consignee to apply to this agent for a commodity inspection. The report issued by BURMESTER·DUNCKER&JOLY, incorporating findings from relevant inspection agencies, indicated that 250 cases of black tea loaded in container HTMU-5005420 were contaminated by the odor of refined naphthalene. It was later ascertained in Shanghai that the container numbered HTMU-5005420 had carried refined naphthalene on a previous voyage from France to Shanghai, and that the current voyage loaded exactly 250 cases of black tea in this container. The survey report issued by BURMESTER·DUNCKER&JOLY in Hamburg was entirely consistent with the facts subsequently investigated in Shanghai. It should be determined that the residual odor of refined naphthalene from the previous voyage of container HTMU-5005420 was the sole source of contamination for the 250 cases of black tea on this voyage. A representative of the carrier was also present during the inspection of the goods. BURMESTER·DUNCKER&JOLY's measures in handling the contaminated tea were reasonable and in line with international practice, and thus the survey report it issued could be accepted. The Ocean Shipping Company's contentions that the cause of contamination was unclear, that the inspection report by the Plaintiff's agent in Hamburg did not correspond with the actual situation, and that the Plaintiff had lightly compensated the insured, lacked factual basis and were not supported.

According to international practice, containers should be clean, dry, free of residue, and free of persistent odors left by previous cargoes. The bill of lading issued by the Ocean Shipping Company was subject to the "Hague Rules," which require that the carrier shall, before and at the beginning of the voyage, exercise due diligence to make the holds, refrigerating and cool chambers, and all other parts of the ship in which goods are carried, fit and safe for their reception, carriage, and preservation. Moreover, the two Defendants had agreements in container transport on other routes providing that the Ocean Shipping Company should, five days before loading into the ship's hold, provide clean, dry, odor-free, and intact empty containers at the port terminal yard for delivery onto the transport vehicles of the Shanghai Branch. According to the domestic practice for container transport, the carrier should guarantee the provision of containers suitable for carriage. The Ocean Shipping Company's argument that, under FCL conditions, the container should be regarded as the packaging of the goods could not be accepted; rather, it should correctly be considered as "all other parts of the ship in which goods are carried" as expressed in the Hague Rules. As the carrier providing the containers, knowing that the shipper was shipping tea, which is highly susceptible to tainting by odors, it delivered to the shipper an unsuitable container that had not been thoroughly cleaned and still retained the odor of the previous voyage's cargo. This violated Article 111 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China regarding "failure to fulfill contractual obligations as agreed," and constituted negligence on the part of the carrier, which should bear liability for compensating the damage to the tea.

The transport conditions for the three containers under bill of lading CS432SSK-B173, issued by the agent of the Defendant Ocean Shipping Company, were FCL, meaning the Defendant Shanghai Branch, as the shipper's full agent, handled the dispatch, counting, loading, and sealing of the containers. Although at the time the State Administration for Commodity Inspection had not explicitly stipulated statutory inspection for containers used for tea, Article 5 of the "Rules for Container Inspection" formulated by the State Administration for Commodity Inspection provided that, besides statutory inspection, "parties involved in foreign trade may, as needed, apply to the local commodity inspection authority for inspection of cargo loading and unloading in containers," with inspection items including assessment of container suitability for carriage, cleanliness, and other individual items. The Shanghai Branch knew that inspecting the container was its duty as the shipper's agent; however, before loading the tea on this voyage, the Shanghai Branch did not apply for commodity inspection, believing it had sufficient confidence in the suitability of the containers for loading. According to Clause 12 on the reverse side of the Ocean Shipping Company's bill of lading, for containers loaded by the shipper, the shipper shall be responsible if the unsuitability or deficiency of the container was apparent on reasonable inspection by the shipper prior to or at the time of loading. Although at the time of the incident there were no clear regulations governing container management, the general principles of container management, as reflected in current domestic provisions, were consistent: the carrier should provide the loading party with containers in good technical condition. The loading party should carefully inspect the container body before loading; containers that cannot ensure the safety of the goods should not be used. The standard for the handover of empty containers required: container body intact, watertight, no light leakage, clean, dry, odor-free, and with clear container number and loading specifications. The substance causing the contamination in this case was the odor of refined naphthalene that had not been completely eliminated after the previous voyage of container HTMU-5005420. Refined naphthalene is a toxic chemical industrial product; its pungent odor is noticeable and can be detected by an ordinary person. After a voyage lasting over a month, when the goods arrived in Hamburg, a strong odor was still emitted. Therefore, it was difficult to accept the Shanghai Branch's claim that it had not detected any special odor inside the container before loading. The Shanghai Branch, as the shipper's agent responsible for loading and sealing, failed to fulfill its duty to carefully inspect the container body before loading. This violated Article 66, Paragraph 2 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC, and constituted fault based on overconfidence or negligence, for which it should also bear liability for compensation for the cargo damage in this case.

In summary, the Ocean Shipping Company, in violation of relevant regulations and international practice, negligently provided an unsuitable container, resulting in the contamination of the tea. The Shanghai Branch failed to carefully inspect the container body in accordance with routine practice, and due to overconfidence or negligence, contributed to the actual occurrence of the tea contamination. Pursuant to Article 112, Paragraph 1 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC, the Ocean Shipping Company should bear the greater part of the liability for compensation, and the Shanghai Branch should correspondingly bear a certain part of the liability.

Accordingly, the Shanghai Maritime Court rendered its judgment on August 22, 1991:

1. The Defendant Ocean Shipping Company shall bear 60% of the liability for the tea contamination, and compensate the Plaintiff £4,485.98, 1,128.60 German marks, and interest losses of £2,025.53 and 303.10 German marks;

2. The Defendant Shanghai Branch shall bear 40% of the liability for the tea contamination, and compensate the Plaintiff £2,990.65, 752.40 German marks, and interest losses of £1,350.35 and 202.06 German marks;

3. The above sums shall be paid in full within ten days from the day following the effective date of this judgment. In case of delay, the late payment penalty shall be calculated in accordance with the settlement rules of the People's Bank of China.

Court acceptance fee of RMB 552.09 and other litigation costs of RMB 500, totaling RMB 1,052.09, shall be borne by the Defendant Ocean Shipping Company in the amount of RMB 631.25 and by the Defendant Shanghai Branch in the amount of RMB 420.84.

After the first instance judgment was pronounced, the Defendant Ocean Shipping Company objected and appealed to the Shanghai High People's Court.

Appellant's Arguments

The Appellant Ocean Shipping Company argued: The container release order issued by the carrier did not include the container number; the party taking delivery of the container was the shipper's agent, China National Foreign Trade Transportation Corporation, Shanghai Branch. Tea belongs to the category of foodstuffs; the shipper's agent did not inspect the empty container before loading, so the responsibility for the residual odor contamination of the tea should be borne by the Shanghai Branch. The shipper's claim against the carrier exceeded the time limit specified in the bill of lading, and the claim of the Zhejiang Branch should not be supported. Even if the carrier were liable for this matter, it should be entitled to limitation of liability under the bill of lading. The consignee indicated on this bill of lading was inconsistent with the actual person taking delivery of the goods. The status of the Zhejiang Branch as the assignee of the shipper's rights should be reexamined. It requested the reversal of the original judgment and the dismissal of any liability on the part of the Appellant.

Appellee Zhejiang Branch's Arguments

The Appellee Zhejiang Branch argued: The Appellee filed a claim with the carrier within the one-year period and received confirmation; according to the terms of the bill of lading and the agreement between the People's Insurance Company of China Head Office and the Ocean Shipping Company Head Office, it should be considered that the time limit was not lost. The bill of lading provided that the carrier's period of responsibility was from after loading until before discharge. The contamination of the tea in this case occurred before loading. The Appellant's raising of the defense of "limitation of liability" at the second instance was clearly unreasonable. The bill of lading issued by the carrier was an order bill of lading; the consignee held the original insurance policy endorsed by transfer. Upon arrival of the goods at the port of destination, a joint inspection was organized by representatives of the cargo interests, the vessel, and the insurer's agent. Therefore, the insurer's litigation status was beyond question. It requested that the original judgment be affirmed.

Appellee Shanghai Branch's Arguments

The Appellee Shanghai Branch argued: The Appellant, as the nominal container supplier, had the obligation to provide empty containers suitable for carriage. Failure to provide clean, odor-free empty containers constituted a breach of contract. There were no regulations requiring statutory inspection of containers used for loading tea; the Shanghai Branch had no duty to inspect the container. Refined naphthalene is a volatile substance; only after a long period in a sealed container would it emit residual odors. The Shanghai Branch did not detect any peculiar smell before loading. The original judgment's finding that the Shanghai Branch bore partial liability for the tea contamination lacked factual basis.

The Shanghai High People's Court held: The carrier in maritime container transport, upon accepting the shipper's application for carriage, is obliged to satisfy the shipper's requirement by providing clean, dry, odor-free, and suitable empty containers for the carriage of the goods. The contamination of the tea in this case was caused by the residual odor of refined naphthalene inside the container. The facts proved that one of the containers provided by the Appellant had indeed carried refined naphthalene before. By putting into use an empty container that had not been thoroughly cleaned, the Appellant bore responsibility for the container's unsuitability for carriage. As this responsibility did not arise during the course of the voyage, the Appellant could not enjoy the defense of "limitation of liability." After the incident, the agents of the consignee and the insurer, together with the carrier, had conducted an inspection of the tea at the port of discharge; at that time, the carrier did not raise any objection to the identity of the consignee and the insurer. The Appellant's argument at the second instance for a reexamination of the assignee of rights was baseless. The time limits within which the Appellee Zhejiang Branch filed its claim and instituted the lawsuit did not exceed the periods stipulated in the bill of lading and the agreement; the Appellant's appellate argument that the time limit had been lost was not sustainable. The original judgment's findings of fact and apportionment of liability were not erroneous, and its application of the relevant articles of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC was correct and should be affirmed. Accordingly, the Shanghai High People's Court, pursuant to Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (1) and Article 232 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered judgment:

The original judgment was affirmed, and the appeal was dismissed.

The court acceptance fee of RMB 552.09 for the second instance was to be borne by the Appellant, Guangzhou Ocean Shipping Company.
